question: What has changed for first-line treatment of metastatic EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer since 2024-06-01?

baseline.answer: Since June 2024, first-line treatment of metastatic EGFR-mutant NSCLC has shifted toward combination strategies. Amivantamab plus lazertinib was FDA approved for first-line treatment of EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R NSCLC based on MARIPOSA, showing a 7.1-month improvement in median progression-free survival and a 30% reduction in the risk of progression or death versus osimertinib. Overall survival improvements seen in FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA have led many oncologists to use combination regimens for most patients as first-line therapy. Osimertinib monotherapy still retains a role in older, fragile patients or those with favorable prognostic features such as absence of EGFR mutation in plasma and TP53 wild-type status because of its better safety profile. The NorthStar trial also suggested that adding local consolidation therapy, such as radiation or surgery, to first-line osimertinib monotherapy may improve progression-free survival.

search_results.title: Polling Data Show Updates in Treatment of mNSCLC With EGFR Mutations | Targeted Onc - Immunotherapy, Biomarkers, and Cancer Pathways
search_results.content: Recently, 2 new combination therapies have been FDA approved. First, amivantamab-vmjw (Rybrevant) plus lazertinib (Lazcluze) was approved for first-line treatment of locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC (mNSCLC) harboring EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R mutations based on findings from the phase 3 MARIPOSA trial (NCT04487080).8 Trial results showed a 7.1-month improvement in median progression-free survival and a 30% reduction in the risk of progression or death with the combination vs patients treated with osimertinib.8 Second, based on findings from the phase 3 MARIPOSA-2 trial (NCT04988295), the FDA approved amivantamab plus chemotherapy (carboplatin and pemetrexed [Alimta]) for patients with locally advanced or mNSCLC harboring EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R mutations

search_results.title: As Practice-Changing Data Hit EGFR-Mutated NSCLC Care, What’s Next?
search_results.content:
The following interview was lightly edited and condensed for space, style, and clarity.

Oncology News Central (ONC): One of the biggest stories in EGFR-mutated NSCLC care in 2025 was the improvement in overall survival seen with several different drug combinations. What questions remain about these regimens?

Zosia Piotrowska, MD, MHS: I think that’s the biggest story in EGFR-mutated NSCLC care this year. Although there was some initial hesitation about these different combination strategies and the balance of toxicity and efficacy, I think that the overall survival improvements that we saw in both FLAURA2 and MARIPOSA have changed practice and have made us use combination strategies for most patients as first-line therapy. [...] Dr. Piotrowska: One important piece of data that came out this year was the NorthStar trial from MD Anderson, which was presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Annual Congress this year. It showed that adding local consolidation therapy, whether that be radiation or in some cases even surgery, to patients with EGFR-mutated lung cancer on first-line osimertinib monotherapy seemed to improve progression-free survival. There are a lot of open questions about which patients benefit most, what sites of disease should be treated, and what types of local consolidative therapy should be used and when. But I think overall, this idea of adding not just systemic therapy but thinking about other kinds of therapeutic approaches that may improve outcomes for our patients is really [...] Dr. Piotrowska: Of course it does – absolutely. I think that we are using more of our effective drugs upfront, and that leaves an unmet need in that second- and later-line setting. Certainly, patients who get first-line osimertinib monotherapy can access amivantamab in combination with chemotherapy in the second line. But if we use either the MARIPOSA or the FLAURA2 regimen upfront, it is more of an open question as to what the optimal second-line therapy is.
